notes.addressCollisionWithTestnet: Several of these addresses also exist on testnet 46630 holding different contracts — EligibleRegistry, EventCalendar and PriceCommitter are identical strings on both chains, and this mainnet ScreeningVerifier shares an address with testnet's UnshieldVerifier. That is CREATE doing what it does: same deployer, same nonce, same address. Nothing disambiguates them but the chain id, so never copy an address between the two deployment files, and never read one of these on the wrong RPC and believe the answer.
notes.quoteAsset: USDG at its real address, registered as the STABLE kind before the pool was deployed so the pool's immutable quoteAssetId could be the id the registry returned rather than one typed into an environment variable.
notes.assets: All 35 Robinhood tokenized equities that have a Chainlink feed, registered through the ordinary registerAsset path — no bypass, no relaxed check, nothing skipped. The pairs were derived by scripts/mainnet-asset-pairs.mjs from the same two sources the dashboard reads.
notes.pricingCap: PriceCommitter.MAX_ASSETS is 32 and 35 equities are registered, so no window can price the whole universe. The pricer selects the assets a window actually has orders for, which is both the fix and the intended optimisation.
notes.custody: Verified on a fork of this chain before deploying: a pooled contract can hold these tokens, is not on TokenControl's blocklist, and is credited the exact raw amount sent. See contracts/test/MainnetCustody.t.sol.
notes.roles: The relayer 0x2612fF20d96d53761032AF41BD161055992c5B2E holds SEALER_ROLE and SETTLER_ROLE on the pool and PRICER_ROLE on the committer, and holds neither admin, GOV nor GUARDIAN on either — verified on chain rather than taken from the deploy script's own output.
notes.verification: All seven contracts are verified on Sourcify at exact_match, creation and runtime bytecode both — https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/4663/<address>. Not on Blockscout: robinhoodchain.blockscout.com sits behind a Cloudflare challenge that returns an HTML interstitial to forge verify-contract and to Sourcify's own forwarder (403), so that route needs the explorer's web UI. Sourcify is an independent check and the stronger one to cite anyway, since it matches deployed bytecode rather than trusting an explorer's record of it.
notes.redeploy: v2, block 70,575,648. PriceCommitter v1 deferred any asset whose effectiveAt was non-zero — the timestamp of the *last* multiplier change, so in the past for anything ever restated. That deferred 13 of 35 assets permanently, AAPL GOOGL META NVDA and SPY among them, while assets nobody had restated crossed normally. RwaDarkPool.pricer is immutable, so the fix meant a new pool; the registry, calendar and all three verifiers were reused, which is why it cost 10.4M gas rather than 42M. Verified after: 35 of 35 assets report flags 0 against the new committer, 22 of 35 against the old one.
notes.shieldGate: v2's pool is deployed with shieldVerifier = address(0) from its constructor. v1 was deployed with a real screening verifier while no circuit was compiled and no attestation issuer existed, so every deposit reverted with InvalidProof; it was turned off with setVerifiers after the fact. Reinstate when an issuer exists.
notes.batchVerifier: Redeployed 2026-09-24 after the batch_cross circuit was corrected: the per-order price selector was one-hot across all 32 table rows without proving the chosen row was one the committed root covers, so a price in a trailing row could drive a trade it never priced. A circuit change is a new verification key, and a proof from the new circuit is rejected by the old verifier with SumcheckFailed. The pool follows via setVerifiers; the retired verifier stays deployed so a proof already in flight against it can still be checked. Confirmed on chain: the new address verifies a real proof from the fixed circuit, the old one rejects it, and a perturbed public input is rejected.
notes.pool: v3, deployed 2026-09-24 at block 71095650. Three findings from the public-source review, all of which change RwaDarkPool and therefore ship together rather than as three redeploys each stranding notes in the last pool. (1) Withdrawal verification was skipped when the verifier was the zero address and the setter accepted zero, so one governance call turned a proof-gated exit into an unproven one; it is unconditional now and setVerifiers refuses both a zero and an address with no code. (2) Published output commitments were emitted beside the proven subtree root with nothing binding them, so a settler could publish leaves a recipient could not build a path from; the contract folds them and refuses a mismatch. (3) Queued deposits drained only from settleBatch and voidWindow, 32 at a time, so past the 32nd a holder had no path and could not withdraw; drainPendingDeposits is permissionless and bounded. Verified on the deployed contract: zeroing the withdrawal verifier reverts WithdrawalVerifierRequired, a codeless one reverts VerifierHasNoCode, the drain exists and reverts NothingQueued on an empty queue, and every byte of the runtime code matches this build apart from immutables and the metadata hash. The v2 pool accepted a zero withdrawal verifier, which is what the finding said.
notes.retiredPools: v1 and v2. Notes in either stay withdrawable from the pool that holds them: unshield carries no pause, no role and no window check, and their verifiers are untouched. The vault scans them so a balance never silently disappears.
notes.disclosureRegistry: Deployed 2026-09-24. Governance is the deployer. No auditor is registered and that is deliberate: registering one publishes an encryption key that disclosures get sealed to, and a placeholder nobody holds the secret for would be a trusted-looking recipient that can never read anything. Until a real auditor is registered, grant() reverts with UnknownAuditor and the dashboard says so -- sealing a viewing key needs none of this and works regardless; the registry is the public, revocable record that a grant happened.
